newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Stasi officers accused of aiding guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Stasi officers accused of aiding guerrillas.

text.p: Four former East German intelligence officers went on trial on Wednesday on charges of helping some of West Germany's most wanted guerrillas start new lives in the Communist state and escape justice in the West.

The accused, Harry Dahl, 67, chief of the counter-terrorism department in the feared Ministry for State Security (Stasi) and three officers, Guenter Jaeckel, 62, Hans-Hermann Petzold, 52 and Gerd Zaumseil, 48, were accused of prevention of justice.

The sensational case is the latest to try to determine how far East Berlin supported international terrorism and punish those behind an "unholy alliance" between the Stasi and the leftist Red Army Faction (RAF), that struck fear into the West German establishment during the 1970s and 1980s.

"They are charged with giving RAF members false identities, financial support, flats and work to assimilate them into everyday life in East Germany from 1980 to 1990," prosecutor Helmut Altenbuchner-Koenigsdorfer said.
"In this way they prevented the terrorists from being brought to justice in West Germany," he told the court.

Former East German citizens can usually only be punished for deeds in the Communist country under East German law, but this case was different, he argued: "The accused acted in East Germany but their actions had their effect in West Germany."
Defence lawyers in the case say their clients do not dispute they helped to give the retired guerrillas a new start in life, but deny preventing the course of justice.
"Our clients did not actively support terrorism, they took the terrorists out of circulation and helped them lead normal lives," said Petzold's lawyer, Manfred Studier.
Studier argued that even if they were deemed guilty of preventing justice, they had committed a lesser offence to prevent a more serious crime -- that of further bomb attacks.

"The RAF members asked to be taken in. We did not approve of their deeds, but their anti-capitalist stance was close to our socialist views," Dahl told the court. "We wanted to prevent a terrorist scene developing in East Germany."
He argued that no political or security damage was done to West or East Germany: "On the contrary, jailing them would have led to more attacks. We closed the vicious circle".
The guerrillas were taken in on orders from former Stasi chief Erich Mielke. "Such an explosive case could not have been decided without the head of state Erich Honecker," Dahl added.

The arrests of the 10 guerrillas in summer 1990 shocked Germans on both sides of the Cold War divide and prompted many to ponder what the proponents of armed revolutionary struggle had in common with the rulers of a stagnant Communist regime.
Defence lawyers in the case say the Stasi milked them for information on their methods in return for a new life.

Some of the guerrillas were regarded as some of West Germany's most dangerous criminals. Susanne Albrecht had been wanted for her part in the 1977 murder of banker Juergen Ponto, the chairman of Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt.
Silke Maier-Witt and Monika Helbing were wanted in connection with the 1977 kidnapping and murder of Employers' Federation chief Hanns-Martin Schleyer and other RAF attacks.

Eight were convicted and sentenced to between six yeras and six months and 13 years jail. Two were freed because the statute of limitations on their alleged crimes had run out. Inge Viett, the last to be freed, left jail last month.
Their lives as ordinary East German citizens working and bringing up families was one of the best-kept secrets of the Cold War -- thanks to the four ex-Stasi officers.
The case may hinge on whether federal law can be applied in the former East German officers' case -- something the court must decide. A conviction can mean up to five years in jail.
